key_terms.meaning: A memoryless element whose output at any instant depends only on the present input, and not linearly on it: y = f(x), with f not a straight line through the origin.
y = kx while |x| ≤ a, and y = ±ka once |x| > a; the gain falls to zero for large signals.
y = 0 for |x| ≤ a and y = k(x − a·sgn x) beyond; small signals produce no output at all.
A hysteresis loop of half-width b: the output keeps its old value until the input moves past b, so the effective gain is amplitude-dependent and has phase lag.
The complex ratio of the fundamental component of the output to a sinusoidal input of amplitude A: N(A) = Y₁∠φ₁ ÷ A, with ω dropped out.

key_terms.term: Describing function of an ideal relay
key_terms.meaning: For a relay switching between +M and −M, N(A) = 4M/(πA): the effective gain shrinks as the amplitude grows.
The x₁–x₂ plane for a second-order system, with x₁ = x and x₂ = ẋ; the family of solution curves drawn in it is the phase portrait.
A point where f(x₁, x₂) = 0, so the state stays there forever if placed there exactly.
Shapes of trajectories near an equilibrium of a linear second-order system; these depend on whether the eigenvalues of A are real or complex, and on the signs of their real parts.
An isolated closed trajectory: paths on one side spiral onto it (or away), so the system settles into an oscillation of fixed amplitude and frequency decided by the system itself.
A limit cycle that attracts neighbouring trajectories; an unstable one repels them, and a semi-stable one attracts from one side only.
A scalar function, positive definite and zero only at the equilibrium, that does not increase along any trajectory; it acts like an energy.
For every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 with ‖x(0)‖ < δ giving ‖x(t)‖ < ε for all t ≥ 0; trajectories stay near, but need not approach, the equilibrium.
Stable and also x(t) → 0 as t → ∞ for all starts close enough to the origin.
Asymptotically stable for every initial state in the whole state space, not just a neighbourhood.
V(x) → ∞ as ‖x‖ → ∞; needed, along with V̇ < 0, to extend a local stability proof to the whole space.
A recipe: with Jacobian J(x) = ∂f/∂x, find a constant positive definite P such that JᵀP + PJ is negative definite; then the origin is asymptotically stable.
AᵀP + PA = −Q; for a stable A and any positive definite Q it has a unique positive definite solution P, which can serve as a quadratic Lyapunov function.
A scalar measuring how bad a control is, e.g. J = ∫₀^∞ (xᵀQx + uᵀRu) dt, with Q ≥ 0 weighting state error and R > 0 weighting control effort.
The optimal state feedback u = −Kx that minimises a quadratic cost for a linear plant ẋ = Ax + Bu, with K = R⁻¹BᵀP and P the solution of the Riccati equation.

takeaways: Real elements lose their fixed gain once the signal is large, small, or reversed in direction, and saturation, dead zone and backlash are the three common shapes of that loss.
The describing function N(A) buys a frequency-domain test at the price of assuming a sinusoidal input, a single nonlinear block and good low-pass filtering by the linear part.
In a phase portrait the geometry is the answer: spirals mean oscillation with decay, closed curves mean sustained oscillation, and saddles mean a direction of escape.
A limit cycle is self-excited and amplitude-fixed by the system, unlike the undamped linear oscillator whose amplitude comes from the initial condition.
A Lyapunov function proves stability by showing an energy-like quantity always falls, so no differential equation has to be solved.
The Lyapunov equation AᵀP + PA = −Q turns the search for a quadratic Lyapunov function into a linear matrix equation.
Optimal control states the goal as a cost and lets the mathematics pick the control, instead of tuning gains by hand.
For a linear plant with a quadratic cost the optimal control is always a linear state feedback u = −Kx, so LQR is the workhorse of modern design.
The weights Q and R are the design knobs: larger Q gives faster, harder control, larger R gives a gentler control that uses less effort.
bank_note: Long answers usually begin with the standard definition and a labelled sketch of the nonlinearity, then move to the analytical step — the N(A) formula, the phase portrait, the Lyapunov candidate, or the Riccati solution — and finish with a comment on what the result means physically.

bank.q: Define a static nonlinearity. Sketch and explain saturation, dead zone and backlash, and state what each one does to the gain and phase of a closed loop.
outline: Definition: output depends only on present input, y = f(x), f nonlinear.
Saturation sketch and equation; gain falls from k to ka/A for large A.
Dead zone sketch; no output for small signals, so low-amplitude oscillation is unnoticed.
Backlash sketch as a hysteresis loop; gain drop plus phase lag, and it is not a single-valued function of x.
Effect: reduced open-loop gain and extra lag — poorer phase margin, possible limit cycling.

bank.q: Explain the describing function method: its definition, the assumptions behind it, and why N depends on amplitude A but not on frequency ω.
outline: Input A sin ωt to a single static nonlinearity; output is periodic, expand in Fourier series.
N(A) = complex ratio of the fundamental output to the input.
Assumptions: odd nonlinearity, one nonlinear block, linear part acts as a low-pass filter so higher harmonics are attenuated, no subharmonics.
Why amplitude only: a memoryless element has no frequency dependence, and a sinusoidal steady state leaves only amplitude as the free variable.

bank.q: For a second-order autonomous system ẋ₁ = x₂, ẋ₂ = f(x₁, x₂), define equilibrium points and explain how the eigenvalues of the Jacobian classify them as node, focus, centre or saddle.
outline: Autonomous means t does not appear explicitly; trajectories do not cross.
Equilibrium points from f = 0.
Linearise about the point, get matrix A and its eigenvalues.
Real eigenvalues of the same sign: node; opposite signs: saddle; complex with nonzero real part: focus; purely imaginary: centre.
Stability from the sign of the real parts; saddle is always unstable.

bank.q: Define a limit cycle. Distinguish stable, unstable and semi-stable limit cycles, and contrast a limit cycle with the oscillation of an undamped linear system.
outline: Isolated closed trajectory in the phase plane; neighbouring paths do not close.
Stable: nearby paths spiral in; unstable: spiral out; semi-stable: in from one side, out from the other.
Amplitude and frequency are fixed by the system, not by initial conditions.
Linear undamped oscillator: a continuum of closed curves, amplitude set by initial state, and it is not isolated.

bank.q: A relay with output ±M drives a linear plant G(s) = 1/[s(s+1)(s+2)]. Using the describing function, find the amplitude and frequency of the predicted limit cycle.
outline: N(A) = 4M/(πA); find the phase-crossover frequency of G(jω) where ∠G = −180°.
At that ω, |G(jω)| = 1/(ω·√(ω²+1)·√(ω²+4)) with ω = √2.
Limit cycle condition G(jω)N(A) = −1, i.e. N(A) = 1/|G(jω)|.
Solve 4M/(πA) = 1/|G(jω)| for A.
Check stability of the cycle by perturbing A and seeing whether the intersection moves back.

bank.q: Derive the describing function of a saturation element with slope k and saturation level a, and use it to explain why a high-gain loop with saturation can oscillate.
outline: Output is periodic and odd; integrate over one quarter cycle.
N(A) = k for A ≤ a; N(A) = (2k/π)[sin⁻¹(a/A) + (a/A)√(1 − (a/A)²)] for A > a.
N falls monotonically from k to 0 as A grows; the effective open-loop gain shrinks with amplitude.
Where the Nyquist plot of the linear part cuts the −1/N(A) locus, a limit cycle is predicted.
Physical reading: the loop is stable for small signals and for very large ones but may settle at an in-between amplitude.

bank.q: Draw the phase portrait of ẍ + 0.6ẋ + x = 0 and of ẍ + x = 0, and label singular points and trajectory shapes.
outline: State variables x₁ = x, x₂ = ẋ; write the two first-order equations.
Eigenvalues of the matrix for the damped case: −0.3 ± j0.954, complex with negative real part, so the origin is a stable focus.
Damped case: inward spirals.
Undamped case: eigenvalues ±j, centre, closed curves, amplitude from initial conditions.
Isocline method as a sketching aid.

bank.q: Show that V(x) = x₁² + x₂² proves asymptotic stability of the origin for ẋ₁ = x₂, ẋ₂ = −x₁ − x₂.
outline: V is positive definite and radially unbounded.
V̇ = 2x₁ẋ₁ + 2x₂ẋ₂ = 2x₁x₂ + 2x₂(−x₁ − x₂) = −2x₂².
V̇ ≤ 0 only, not strictly negative definite; use LaSalle or note V̇ = 0 only on the line x₂ = 0, where ẋ₂ = −x₁ ≠ 0 unless x₁ = 0.
Hence no whole trajectory stays in V̇ = 0 except the origin, so the origin is asymptotically stable.
Radial unboundedness makes it global.

bank.q: For A = [[0, 1], [−2, −3]], B = [[0],[1]], Q = I, R = 1, solve the Riccati equation and find the LQR gain K.
outline: Write P = [[p₁₁, p₁₂],[p₁₂, p₂₂]] and substitute into AᵀP + PA − PBR⁻¹BᵀP + Q = 0.
Three scalar equations in p₁₁, p₁₂, p₂₂.
Solve, keeping the positive definite root.
K = R⁻¹BᵀP gives the feedback gains.
Check that A − BK is stable by its eigenvalues.

bank.q: Use the Krasovskii method to test asymptotic stability of ẋ₁ = x₂, ẋ₂ = −x₂ − x₁³ at the origin.
outline: Form the Jacobian J(x) = [[0, 1],[−3x₁², −1]].
Choose P = I and compute JᵀP + PJ = [[−6x₁², 0],[0, −2]].
Matrix is negative definite for x₁ ≠ 0; at the origin it becomes negative definite too.
Conclusion: origin is asymptotically stable.
Note Krasovskii gives a sufficient condition only — failing it proves nothing.

bank.q: Compare describing function analysis with phase plane analysis: what each can handle, what each assumes, and which questions each answers best.
outline: DF: frequency domain, higher-order systems, one static nonlinearity, sinusoidal-input assumption, predicts limit cycle amplitude and frequency, cannot show transient or multiple equilibria.
Phase plane: exact for second order, no sinusoidal assumption, shows global picture, transients, separatrices; limited to two state variables and often graphical.
DF is approximate and quantitative; phase plane is exact and qualitative.
Use DF to predict oscillation of a loop with a valve or relay; use phase plane to see whether a start point escapes to another equilibrium.
Both are tools for suspicion plus design, not substitutes for simulation.

bank.q: State the Lyapunov stability theorems. Explain why a Lyapunov function proving stability is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one, and why radial unboundedness is needed for the global claim.
outline: Stability: V positive definite, V̇ ≤ 0 locally. Asymptotic: V̇ negative definite.
Sufficiency: finding one V settles the question; failing to find one settles nothing.
Conditions are sufficient because many V may exist, and a bad guess can fail on a stable system.
Global claim needs V̇ < 0 for all x and V(x) → ∞ as ‖x‖ → ∞, otherwise trajectories can escape to infinity while V stays bounded.
Example: V = x₁²/(1 + x₁²) type functions that fail radial unboundedness.

bank.q: Explain the linear quadratic regulator. Justify the form u = −Kx, derive the Riccati equation, and discuss how Q and R affect the closed-loop response.
outline: Plant ẋ = Ax + Bu, cost J = ∫₀^∞ (xᵀQx + uᵀRu) dt with Q ≥ 0, R > 0.
Hamiltonian or completion-of-squares argument gives u = −R⁻¹BᵀPx.
P solves AᵀP + PA − PBR⁻¹BᵀP + Q = 0, the algebraic Riccati equation; P ≥ 0 for stabilisable and detectable systems.
Increasing Q makes the state decay faster at the cost of larger u; increasing R penalises effort and slows the response.
Gain margin and robustness properties of LQR; LQR is optimal for the stated model, so model error still matters.

bank.q: A pendulum model ẋ₁ = x₂, ẋ₂ = −sin x₁ − 0.2x₂ is given. Find all equilibrium points, sketch the phase portrait near each, and use a Lyapunov argument to discuss the stability of the hanging position.
outline: Equilibria at x₂ = 0 and sin x₁ = 0, i.e. x₁ = 0, ±π, ±2π, …
Jacobian [[0,1],[−cos x₁, −0.2]]; at x₁ = 0 eigenvalues have negative real part, stable focus.
At x₁ = π the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs: saddle, so the upright position is unstable.
Energy candidate V = (1 − cos x₁) + x₂²/2 is positive definite near the origin and V̇ = −0.2x₂² ≤ 0.
LaSalle plus the damping argument gives asymptotic stability of the hanging position; no limit cycle exists because the damping removes energy everywhere except the equilibrium.

glossary.def: A system whose response does not obey superposition, so its behaviour depends on the size and sign of the input and on the starting state.
A memoryless nonlinear element whose output at an instant is a fixed function of the input at that same instant.
A nonlinearity whose output stops growing once the input passes a limit, so the incremental gain becomes zero.
A range of input around zero for which the output stays zero, common in valves and gears with slack.
A hysteresis-type nonlinearity caused by looseness in a mechanical linkage, where the output lags the input by a fixed gap.
An amplitude-dependent complex gain equal to the fundamental component of the output divided by a sinusoidal input.
Another name for the describing function method, because the nonlinearity is replaced by a gain at the fundamental frequency.
The plane whose axes are the two states of a second-order autonomous system.
The complete picture of trajectories of a system drawn in the phase plane.
The curve traced by the state of a system as time runs, plotted in the state space.
A state at which all derivatives are zero, so the system remains there for all time.
An equilibrium with one stable and one unstable direction; paths approach along one line and leave along another.
An equilibrium surrounded by spiralling trajectories that wind inward towards it.
A special trajectory that divides the phase plane into regions with qualitatively different behaviour.
An isolated closed trajectory that neighbouring trajectories approach or leave, giving a self-sustained oscillation.
A positive definite scalar function of the state whose time derivative along the system trajectories is negative or zero.
A function that is zero at the origin and strictly positive everywhere else in a region around it.
A property of a function that grows without limit as the state moves arbitrarily far from the origin in any direction.
An equilibrium where trajectories starting close enough remain close for all future time.
Stability plus the property that nearby trajectories actually converge to the equilibrium.
The linear matrix equation AᵀP + PA = −Q, solved for P to build a quadratic Lyapunov function.
The problem of choosing a control signal that minimises a stated cost while satisfying the plant dynamics.
A scalar integral that scores a control trajectory, usually penalising state error and control effort.
A control signal that is physically allowed and drives the plant from the given start to the required end.
A quadratic matrix equation whose solution gives the optimal feedback gain in LQR and in linear quadratic Gaussian design.
The optimal state-feedback controller for a linear plant with a quadratic performance index.
